Chapter 1: Growing Up in a World Shaped by Injustice
Picture a neighborhood where the air always feels a little heavy—where every street corner tells a story, and history seems to linger in the background. Growing up in New Orleans, life was this unique mix: close-knit families chatting on front porches, laughter echoing through the night, and, at the same time, the shadow of poverty always nearby. The city had its beauty—music that made you want to dance, food that brought people together, and a sense of community that was hard to find anywhere else. But underneath all that was something deeper: a divide that you just couldn’t ignore. For a kid, it became clear pretty early—your skin color could change the way the world treated you, and the rules weren’t always the same for everyone.
Home was a tiny apartment, crowded but somehow cozy—filled with the love of a mother who did everything she could to keep her children safe and fed. She was the anchor, steady as a rock, even when money was tight and the odds seemed stacked against her. The absence of a father left a hole, but her strength became its own lesson—a quiet reminder that even when things are tough, you keep going.
School was supposed to be a place to learn and grow, right? But for a lot of kids, it felt more like a stopgap, a place where dreams rarely made it into the lesson plan. Teachers did their best, but they were stretched thin, and the stories in the textbooks hardly ever reflected the lives of the students sitting in those desks. It was easy to feel like you were invisible—as if the world had already made up its mind about who you could become.
Then came adolescence, and the pull of the streets started to get stronger. There was this sense of belonging you found with friends—people who just got what you were going through. But with that sense of family came real risks. Petty theft, hustling, getting into trouble with the law—it all became part of the daily routine for some. The police were always around, but not in a way that made you feel safe. Instead, every interaction was loaded with suspicion, even hostility, sending a clear message: young Black men were seen as threats, not neighbors.
In that kind of environment, the choices felt pretty limited. Sometimes, grabbing a shot at quick money seemed like the only way to get by, even if it meant putting the hope of a better future on the back burner. But even on the hardest days, there were these small sparks of hope—a neighbor who took the time to share some advice, a teacher who believed in you, or a mother who refused to give up. Tiny gestures, sure, but they planted seeds for something better, even if you couldn’t see it right away.
The city’s racial divisions went way beyond just social circles. Segregation was everywhere, built right into the schools, the parks, even the justice system. The law didn’t feel like it was there to protect you; it felt like it was designed to keep you in your place. Getting arrested was common, and the courts almost never offered second chances. One wrong move, and you could be facing years behind bars, with hardly any hope of turning things around.
And yet, through it all, that desire for dignity and respect never really disappeared. There was a quiet determination burning inside—a need to prove that your worth wasn’t defined by where you were born or what you looked like. That early fight against injustice? It became the foundation for something bigger—not just surviving, but demanding the right to be seen and heard.
